newsitem.title: POLAND: Poles expect criticism from EU, premier not worried.
newsitem.headline: Poles expect criticism from EU, premier not worried.

text.p: A Polish envoy has warned Poland to expect tough criticism when the European Union in July assesses Warsaw's preparations for membership, but the prime minister said on Tuesday the picture was not all bad.

"Let's treat this with calm and a bit more faith in ourselves, in our possiblities and in what has happened to date in Poland," PAP news agency quoted Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz as saying before a cabinet meeting.

The EU's executive, the European Commission, will issue its so-called avis on July 16 and this will have a bearing on its decision in December about which candidate countries should start accession negotiations.

On Monday Jaroslaw Pietras, a Polish vice-minister for EU integration, told a news conference after talks in Brussels that the avis would be highly critical and Polish public opinion should be prepared in advance.

EU officials have repeatedly reproached Warsaw over trade disputes, ranging from the way in which Korea's Daewoo car producer assembles cars in Poland, through protection of its steel industry, down to duties on Scotch whisky.

They have also said Poland is moving too slowly on adjusting its laws to EU standards and expressed concern over the state of such areas as agriculture and the telecoms industry as well as delays in crucial reforms, including that of social security.
Cimoszewicz said no one expected Poland, which embraced democracy in 1989 after four decades of Soviet-style communism, to meet the criteria for EU entry this year, PAP reported.
He added that the opinions Pietras had heard in Brussels were not especially critical in general and that such EU views did not concern Poland alone.
"We realise that in the coming years much will have to changed and reformed in our country, in the economy, the legal system," Cimoszewicz said.
"Our membership will also include the possibility of an elastic moving of the final deadlines for meeting some criteria through the application of transitional periods," he said.
But diplomats from EU countries in Warsaw said that the avis on Poland was likely to include some strong criticism.

One diplomat who asked not to be named said Poland was still seen as part of the leading group among states seeking full membership but it might be ranked behind the Czech Republic and Hungary, which had been more willing to meet EU suggestions.

Poland has its own complaints about the EU, with which it is running a large farm trade deficit. Last week, Warsaw complained that the EU had not carried out an agreement on easing access for Polish soft fruit.
Poland has an association agreement with the EU and hopes to become a member by around 2002.
